Understanding as Compression: Academic and Philosophical Foundations in Human Cognition and Artificial Intelligence

The proposition that "understanding is compression and compression is understanding" is both a philosophical and computational thesis with deep roots in cognitive science, philosophy of mind, and artificial intelligence research. This report surveys foundational and contemporary academic literature that develops and supports the idea that understanding—whether in humans or machines—involves compressing complex information into simpler, more generalizable representations. Key theories and frameworks, such as Kolmogorov complexity, Minimum Description Length (MDL), the Information Bottleneck method, and the role of generative models in cognition and AI, are examined alongside philosophical analyses. Foundational and recent contributions from both theoretical and empirical perspectives are highlighted.

Foundational Theories Linking Understanding and Compression

Andrey Kolmogorov, Ray Solomonoff, and Gregory Chaitin formalized the concept that the complexity of an object (such as a string or dataset) can be measured by the length of the shortest computer program that generates it. This framework, known as Kolmogorov complexity, equates understanding with the ability to compress data into the simplest possible form—intuiting the "program" behind the information. In cognitive terms, learning or generalization can be seen as discovering the shortest (most efficient) models that explain sensory data[1].

Ray Solomonoff extended these ideas in his theory of inductive inference, arguing that prediction and understanding are achieved by inferring the simplest models consistent with observed evidence, thus formalizing the connection between understanding, prediction, and compression[2].

Jorma Rissanen advanced the Minimum Description Length principle, which treats inductive inference as the search for the model that enables the most concise encoding of observed data. MDL is both a statistical method and a theory of understanding: the best explanations are those that compress data most efficiently, balancing simplicity with the ability to account for observed complexity[3]. MDL has influenced both philosophical theories of science and practical approaches in machine learning.

While the thesis that "understanding is compression" has robust theoretical and empirical support, some philosophers and scientists caution against full equivalence. Critics argue that not all forms of understanding reduce solely to compression; contextual, pragmatic, and normative elements (e.g., social meaning, embodied practice) may exceed information-theoretic accounts[12]. Nonetheless, compression remains widely acknowledged as a central (albeit not exclusive) component.

While debates persist about the full adequacy of information-theoretic models, their explanatory power and unifying elegance have established "understanding is compression" as a central and generative concept in both human and machine cognition.

Any agent that learns from its own actions faces one recurring choice: act on what it already knows works, or try something whose payoff is unknown. Exploiting collects the reward that present knowledge can reach. Exploring buys information about rewards the agent cannot yet see. Time or attention spent on one is withheld from the other, and neither can be dropped: an agent that only exploits stays stuck on the best thing it happened to find early, and an agent that only explores never cashes in what it learns.

The tension appears wherever a decision is made repeatedly under uncertainty: a gambler facing a row of slot machines, a lab choosing which experiments to fund, a company weighing refinement of its product against the search for the next one, a reader picking a new book over rereading a loved one, and a knowledge gardener choosing between planting new pages and tending the ones already there.

The formal problem is the multi-armed bandit: a row of slot machines with unknown payout rates and a limited number of pulls to spend on them. Allied statisticians worked on it during the Second World War and found it so hard that Peter Whittle joked it should be dropped on Germany to waste enemy scientists' time. Herbert Robbins gave the problem its standard form in 1952 in "Some aspects of the sequential design of experiments".

In organization theory, James G. March's "Exploration and Exploitation in Organizational Learning" (1991) named the trade-off for firms. Exploitation is refinement, efficiency and execution; exploration is search, variation, risk-taking and discovery. Returns to exploitation are near, certain and fast, while returns to exploration are distant, uncertain and often negative, which is why organizations slide toward exploitation and lose the ability to adapt.

In the balance is written into the algorithms (Exploration–exploitation dilemma, Wikipedia). Epsilon-greedy takes the best-known action most of the time and a random one otherwise. Upper-confidence-bound methods add an optimism bonus to actions tried less often. Thompson sampling draws a guess at each payoff from what has been observed and acts as if the draw were true. Exploration bonuses turn curiosity into a reward of its own, so the agent can exploit it.

Explore early, exploit late. When little is known, information is cheap and there is a long horizon left to use it. As the horizon shortens, the remaining turns are worth more spent on the known best.
Keep exploration cheap and reversible, so a bad draw costs little.
Watch for both failure modes: the settled routine that stopped looking, and the endless survey that never commits.

Seen through cybernetics, a learner is a regulator holding a course through an environment it can only partly see. Exploitation is the corrective action along the known heading. Exploration is the sampling that keeps the map of the environment current, so the corrections stay pointed at the real world. Ashby's requisite variety says a regulator must carry at least as many responses as the world has disturbances, and exploration is how it acquires the variety it lacks. Second-order cybernetics adds the observer to the loop: a gardener steering their own learning is regulating the system that does the steering, which is why the balance is never set once and left alone.

My/Principle/Learn/in Public frames knowledge gardening as calibrating these two forces: exploring adds new things to the garden and new connections to the world, and exploiting tends what is already planted so it becomes more vibrant and real. Explore and Exploit each have a page of their own.
Choosing to exploit means taking the option that present knowledge says pays best, and collecting the reward.
Gains — reward now, with little variance: refinement, efficiency, execution, and the compounding that comes from doing the known thing well.
Costs — the information forgone: untried options stay unknown, and the estimate of the current best goes unchallenged. The map stops being updated while the world keeps changing.

Too far — the settled routine: an agent locked onto the best option it happened to find early, a firm polishing a product after the market has left, a garden that is only ever pruned and never planted.
Choosing to explore means spending a turn on an option whose payoff is unknown, to learn what it is worth.

Gains — information: a truer map of which options pay, and the chance of finding something better than the current best. The value is highest early, when little is known and a long horizon remains to use what is learned.
Costs — the reward forgone on that turn, since the known best was passed over, plus the chance that the unknown option is worse. Returns arrive late and uncertain.

Too far — the perpetual survey: an agent, team or gardener that keeps sampling and never settles, so nothing learned is ever cashed in. March described the result as too many undeveloped ideas and too little distinctive competence.

Team-based agents mark a shift from single-player AI tools—assistants that serve one person, like a personal chief of staff—to agents that act as shared teammates inside a team's existing communication channels, per AI/Concept/Multiplayer/Log/26/09/21 Mon Readwise Summary of Claude Tag.
Instead of living in a private chat with one user, the agent sits at the intersection where a team already comes together: a shared channel that every relevant person can see and add to.

Persistent teammates in carry the whole history of a channel, so no individual has to brief them from scratch. One person's agent-assisted work hands off cleanly to the next person, because the agent's memory of the thread is continuous rather than scoped to a single conversation.

Claude/Tag is Anthropic's instance of this pattern: @-mentioning it in a Slack thread summons a version of Claude that is not tied to any one person, running instead as an organization-scoped teammate with its own permissions, tool access, and persistent memory.

CursorAI/Cloud Agent applies the same pattern to software delivery: mentioning the agent in a Slack channel kicks off work on a collaborative development surface that the whole channel can watch, rather than one developer's private editor.
Org-scoped identity, not personal — permissions, tool access, and memory attach to the team or organization, not to whichever individual happens to type the @-mention.
The conversation is the interface — work happens inside the channel; agents call APIs and run commands in the background, surfacing only the approvals and decisions a human needs to see.
Bounded initiative — a multiplayer agent can take initiative by following up on quiet threads, flagging relevant information, and managing long-horizon tasks without being re-prompted each time.
Division of labor — agents take on the stable, repeatable layers of work, while humans hold the creative and strategic end of the judgment.
Invocation is an @-mention inside an existing channel (@Claude, @cursor) rather than a switch to a separate app; the agent reads the thread it is tagged in for context.

Specialized coworker agents narrow the same pattern to a functional role: an editorial team's agent named Andy collects "nuggets" of story ideas from Slack threads and turns them into newsletter drafts; an always-on product-manager agent keeps a memory.md file tracking priorities and tags a human only when their input is needed.

At company scale, this becomes part of a broader move toward headless software—Salesforce and Slack describe positioning themselves as an agentic OS—where work happens inside the conversation instead of a separate dashboard login.

Context rot is the degradation of an AI/LLM's performance as input length grows, caused by its non-uniform and unreliable handling of extended context.

LLMs have a "context window" that is determined by a maximum number of input s. For a given model, this window affects the upper bound of the complexity of the problem they can handle as well as the amount of private business data that can be utilized in a query.
